name: Xor Filter (xor_singleheader)
workload: Single-threaded membership-test query time vs. space overhead for 10M and 100M random 64-bit keys, 25% of queried keys present, using the fastfilter_cpp bulk-insert-and-query benchmark
claimed_speedup: At 10M keys: Xor8 23ns/query (9.8 bits/key) vs Bloom12 40ns (12.0 bits/key) and Cuckoo12 31ns (12.8 bits/key); Xor16 27ns (19.7 bits/key) vs Bloom16 48ns (16.0 bits/key) and Cuckoo16 32ns (17.0 bits/key). At 100M keys: Xor8 32ns vs Bloom12 58ns and Cuckoo12 38ns (Table 3, Graf & Lemire, JEA 2020)
stars_or_usage: 432 stars; used in production by Databend, ntop nDPI, InfiniFlow, and CockroachDB Pebble
tradeoffs: Immutable once built (no add/remove; must know the full key set upfront); needs a strong ~64-bit hash of the input keys; construction is slower than Bloom/blocked-Bloom (~110-130ns/key vs ~10-40ns/key at 10M keys per Table 2 of the same paper); naturally compressible with gzip/zstd, unlike Bloom/cuckoo.
caveats: Numbers are from the peer-reviewed Journal of Experimental Algorithmics paper (Graf & Lemire 2020), single-threaded, one 2019-era CPU (Skylake); margin over cuckoo filter is modest (23ns vs 31ns) though clearer over Bloom filter (40-48ns). Code is in FastFilter/xor_singleheader and the benchmark harness in FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/FastFilter/xor_singleheader/readme -> linked paper arXiv:1912.08258; cross-checked against FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp benchmark README

name: Binary Fuse Filter (xor_singleheader)
workload: Construction time and bits-per-key for 3-wise and 4-wise binary fuse filters vs. 8/16-bit xor filters, 10^4 to 10^8 random 64-bit keys, single-threaded, 25% of query keys present (Graf & Lemire, JEA 2022)
claimed_speedup: 3-wise binary fuse reaches 9 bits/key (12.5% over theoretical minimum) and 4-wise reaches ~8.6 bits/key (7.5% over minimum) for large sets, vs. xor filter's 9.84 bits/key (23% over minimum); construction of both binary fuse variants is 'more than twice as fast' as xor filter (e.g. ~60ns/key vs ~120-140ns/key at 10^8 keys, Fig. 3a); query time is close to xor filter and faster than cuckoo/Bloom/ribbon/vector-quotient filters in the same test (Fig. 5b, 100M keys, Skylake)
compiler_and_flags: GCC 10, -O3 (adds -march=native for the AVX2-dependent blocked-Bloom baseline)
hardware: Primary: Intel i7-6700 @ 3.4GHz (Skylake), 8MiB L3. Secondary: AMD EPYC 7262 (Zen2, Rome) @ 3.39GHz
stars_or_usage: 432 stars; binary fuse filter is now the recommended/default filter in the repo and is used in production systems (Databend, nDPI, InfiniFlow, CockroachDB Pebble)
tradeoffs: Same immutability constraints as xor filter (must be built from the full key set); for small sets (<20,000 keys) xor filters can be slightly smaller due to lower fixed overhead; requires whole-byte fingerprints (8/16-bit), so isn't tunable to arbitrary false-positive rates.
caveats: Same benchmark suite/authors as the xor filter paper; single-threaded only. Ribbon filters are noted by the same authors as an interesting alternative that also performs well and is worth comparing (see separate Ribbon Filter entry).
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp/readme -> References section -> arXiv:2201.01174

name: BuRR (Ribbon Filter)
workload: Space-overhead comparison of ribbon-filter (retrieval + AMQ) configurations against Bloom, xor, and xor+ filters at varying false-positive rates; best-paper-winning SEA 2022 evaluation (fastfilter_cpp harness)
claimed_speedup: Classic Bloom filters use 1.44*log2(1/f) bits/key (44% over the theoretical minimum); xor filters achieve ~20% overhead and xor+ ~10% for small f; BuRR (ribbon filter) achieves overheads as low as 0.1%, and even speed-optimized configurations stay below 0.5%, while described as having 'extremely low overhead and fast queries'
stars_or_usage: 52 stars; won Best Paper at SEA 2022 (20th International Symposium on Experimental Algorithms)
tradeoffs: Static/immutable retrieval structure (no keys stored, so it cannot enumerate members); construction cost scales worse than hash-table-based filters for very large n; a parallel-construction variant exists on a separate branch.
caveats: The headline space-overhead numbers come from the README and are attributed to the peer-reviewed SEA 2022 paper, but exact hardware/compiler/CPU model were not located in the README itself (would require reading the full LIPIcs paper or preprint to confirm, hence Tier B not A). Primary quantified claim is memory overhead, not raw query latency, though the paper title and abstract also claim fast queries.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos 'ribbon filter' -> lorenzhs/BuRR; cross-referenced via FastFilter binary-fuse-filter paper references [Dillinger & Walzer, arXiv:2103.02515] and FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp README credits

name: Morton Filter
workload: Insertion, deletion, and lookup throughput of a Morton filter (compressed, bandwidth-optimized cuckoo filter) vs. the reference cuckoo filter implementation from Fan et al., as reported in the VLDB 2018 paper
claimed_speedup: Insertion, deletion, and lookup throughputs up to 15.5x, 1.3x, and 2.5x higher than a cuckoo filter respectively, while also using fewer bits per item than a Bloom filter below ~1-3% target false-positive rate
compiler_and_flags: g++ (project recommends g++ 5.4; notes a performance regression in GCC 8.x as of March 2019)
stars_or_usage: 90 stars; developed at AMD Research, published at VLDB 2018 with an extended version in the VLDB Journal (2019)
tradeoffs: Supports self-resizing (grow capacity without a backing structure) unlike vanilla cuckoo filters; requires only a multiple-of-two bucket count rather than a power of two; author explicitly labels the code 'academic-style prototype', not hardened for production.
caveats: The 15.5x/1.3x/2.5x figures are stated in the README, sourced from the authors' own peer-reviewed VLDB paper; exact CPU model and compiler flags used for those specific figures were not confirmed from the README alone (paper PDF was not deep-read for the hardware section), so capped at Tier B. Repo has had no commits in ~5 years.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos 'morton filter' -> AMDComputeLibraries/morton_filter

name: Prefix Filter
workload: Space usage, false-positive rate, operation throughput at varying load, and build time for 0.94*2^28 (~252M) random 64-bit keys at false-positive rate ~2^-8, single-threaded, on an Intel Ice Lake server (PVLDB 15(7), 2022)
claimed_speedup: Overall build time faster than the vector quotient filter and cuckoo filter by 1.39-1.46x and 3.2-3.5x respectively; cuckoo filter's own insertion throughput collapses (a 27x slowdown observed) as occupancy approaches capacity, while prefix filter insertions stay fast; query throughput is comparable to (though about 52%/79% behind, for negative/positive queries) the cuckoo filter at low occupancy; far more space-efficient than the blocked Bloom filter at low target false-positive rates
compiler_and_flags: GCC 10.3.0, Ubuntu 20.04 (specific optimization flags beyond compiler version not stated in the extracted text)
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6336Y (Ice Lake) @ 2.40GHz, 64GiB RAM, 48KiB L1d/1.25MiB L2 per core, 36MiB shared L3
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512 hardware for the fast path; is an incremental filter (supports insertion but the paper focuses on a fixed configured capacity); this is a mixed win, not a strict speed win across every metric.
caveats: IMPORTANT: query throughput is NOT better than the cuckoo filter in this paper's own numbers -- the cuckoo filter is faster for queries at low occupancy (by 52%/79%). Prefix filter's real advantages are build/insertion time and avoiding cuckoo filter's occupancy-dependent insertion collapse, plus much better space efficiency than the blocked Bloom filter. Repo license is Apache-2.0 per LICENSE.md though GitHub's own license detector reports NOASSERTION.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/FastFilter/fastfilter_cpp/readme -> Credits section -> TomerEven/Prefix-Filter; paper arXiv:2203.17139

name: Vacuum Filter
workload: Positive/mixed lookup, insertion, and deletion throughput plus bits-per-item vs. target false-positive rate, 64-bit random keys, varying table occupancy 0-100%, on a DELL workstation (PVLDB 13, 2020)
claimed_speedup: Semi-sorted vacuum filter (VF-ss) is about 1.1x-1.8x faster than semi-sorted cuckoo filter (CF-ss) for positive lookups; vacuum filter has the highest insertion throughput among AMQ structures compared when table occupancy < 65%; vacuum filters use 2-5 fewer bits per item than cuckoo filter, Bloom filter, Morton filter, and counting quotient filter at the same target false-positive rate
hardware: DELL workstation, Intel Xeon E5-2687W @ 3.00GHz, 30MB L3 cache, SK-hynix SC311-S 1TB SSD
tradeoffs: Built on top of / modified from Fan et al.'s cuckoo filter code; the fast implementation is a modified cuckoo filter rather than a from-scratch design; deletion throughput is only 'similar to' cuckoo filter, not better; insertion advantage narrows and eventually loses to cuckoo/vacuum crossover above ~65% occupancy where both slow down comparably.
caveats: CPU model is stated but the paper excerpt read did not contain explicit compiler name/version or optimization flags, so capped at Tier B rather than A. This is peer reviewed (PVLDB) with code public.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos 'vacuum filter' -> wuwuz/Vacuum-Filter; paper at vldb.org/pvldb/vol13/p197-wang.pdf

name: SuRF (Succinct Range Filter)
workload: RocksDB replacement of its Bloom filters with SuRF on a synthetic 100GB time-series dataset (2K simulated sensors, 128-bit keys); end-to-end open-range, closed-range, and worst-case (all-missing-key) point query throughput, SIGMOD 2018 Best Paper
claimed_speedup: Open-range (no upper bound) queries 1.5x faster and closed-range (with upper bound) queries up to 5x faster than RocksDB's original Bloom filter, at equal filter size; but for the worst-case point-query workload (no query keys exist) RocksDB is up to 40% SLOWER using SuRF instead of Bloom filters, because SuRF has a higher false-positive rate at that size (0.2% vs 0.1%)
hardware: Intel Core i7-6770HQ CPU, 32GB RAM, Intel 540s 480GB SSD
stars_or_usage: 554 stars; SIGMOD 2018 Best Paper; evaluated as a RocksDB Bloom-filter replacement
tradeoffs: SuRF trades a higher false-positive rate for the ability to answer range queries and approximate range counts, which plain Bloom filters cannot do at all; for pure point-query, moderate-FPP workloads the paper itself says 'the Bloom filter is usually a better choice than SuRF'; construction speed is comparable to Bloom filter's.
caveats: This is a mixed/nuanced result, not a strict win: SuRF is slower (up to 40%) for point-only, all-miss workloads at equal filter size; its wins (1.5x-5x) are specifically for range queries. Compiler name/flags were not found in the excerpts read (only CPU/RAM/SSD stated), so capped at Tier B.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/efficient/SuRF (found via reasoning about range-filter alternatives to Bloom filter beyond the assignment's seed query); README links SIGMOD best paper
